parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what makes a systematic error different from a random one - it shifts every single reading in the same direction by the same amount, even if you repeat.
parts.proper_answer: Voltmeter has a zero error, e.g. does not read zero with no p.d., or is incorrectly calibrated.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a systematic error means**
Think of a systematic error as a built-in bias in your setup. You are measuring a constant p.d., so if you repeat the reading you get the same wrong value again and again. It cannot be reduced by averaging repeats.

Step 2: **Example for an analogue voltmeter**
A classic example is a zero error. The needle does not sit at zero when the voltage is zero, so every reading is too high or too low by a fixed amount. An incorrectly calibrated scale does the same thing.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what changes slightly from one reading to the next even though the true voltage is constant - something to do with you as the observer.
parts.proper_answer: Parallax error from viewing the needle and scale from different angles, or inconsistent interpolation between scale divisions.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a random error means**
Think of a random error as unpredictable scatter. You are measuring the same constant p.d., but your readings jump a little above and below the true value. Averaging repeats helps here.

Step 2: **Example for an analogue scale**
With an analogue meter you have to line up your eye with the needle. If you look from a slightly different angle each time you get parallax error. Judging the position between two small scale marks slightly differently each time is another random error.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: You know $V$ and $R$ directly, so look for the power relation that links just power, p.d. and resistance.
Hint 2: Substitute $V = 5.0\text{ V}$ and $R = 125\,\Omega$ and check your units give watts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the right power relation**
You have p.d. $V$ and resistance $R$, so the most direct link is: $$P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$ This comes from combining $P = VI$ with $V = IR$.

Step 2: **Substitute and calculate**
Put in the numbers: $$P = \frac{(5.0)^2}{125} = \frac{25}{125} = 0.20\text{ W}$$ Keep 2 significant figures to match the data.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Start by finding the percentage uncertainty in the voltage from $0.1\text{ V}$ in $5.0\text{ V}$.
Hint 2: Think about how the $V^2$ in $P = V^2/R$ affects the uncertainty - what happens to the percentage when a quantity is squared, and how do you then combine it with the $3\%$ in $R$?
parts.proper_answer: Percentage uncertainty in $V = 2\%$, percentage uncertainty in $P = 2 \times 2\% + 3\% = 7\%$
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Percentage uncertainty in V**
Percentage uncertainty is fractional uncertainty x 100: $$\frac{\Delta V}{V} \times 100 = \frac{0.1}{5.0} \times 100 = 2\%$$

Step 2: **Combine for P = V^2 / R**
When a value is raised to a power, multiply its percentage uncertainty by that power. When multiplying or dividing, add the percentages. So: $$\% \text{ uncertainty in } P = 2 \times (\% \text{ in } V) + (\% \text{ in } R)$$ $$ = 2 \times 2\% + 3\% = 7\%$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Convert your $7\%$ back to an absolute spread by finding $7\%$ of your $0.20\text{ W}$ value.
Hint 2: Think about how many decimal places the absolute uncertainty should be quoted to, and how the power value must match it.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the absolute uncertainty**
Percentage uncertainty tells you the fractional spread. Convert it back: $$\Delta P = \frac{7}{100} \times 0.20 = 0.014\text{ W}$$

Step 2: **Round to matching precision**
An absolute uncertainty is normally given to 1 significant figure, so $0.014\text{ W}$ becomes $0.01\text{ W}$. The value must be quoted to the same decimal place, so $0.20\text{ W}$ stays at 2 decimal places: $$P = 0.20 \pm 0.01\text{ W}$$
